knownFor: Bishop of Lyon in Roman Gaul who had heard Polycarp of Smyrna as a boy. About 180 he wrote five books Against Heresies, the fullest answer we still have to the followers of Valentinus. Against their claim to a secret teaching he set three open things: the faith received at baptism, the churches the apostles founded, with their bishops counted one after another, and four Gospels.
datesNote: He gives no year of his own. Eusebius dates the persecution at Lyon to the seventeenth year of the emperor Antoninus Verus, which Arthur McGiffert reckons as 177, under Marcus Aurelius. Eusebius's Chronicle sets it beside 167, and McGiffert argues for 177. He became bishop after Pothinus, and McGiffert thinks not at once but not long after. He wrote the third book of Against Heresies while Eleutherius was bishop of Rome, between 174 and 189 in McGiffert's dates; about 180 is the usual date. His last trace is the quarrel over Easter under Victor of Rome, toward the close of the second century
placeNote: As a boy, lower Asia, the Roman province of Asia, where Polycarp was bishop of Smyrna; then Lyon, in Roman Gaul, on the Rhone, today in France. He says he lived among the Celts
role: Elder and then bishop of the church at Lyon; writer against teachings he held false

keyWorks.title: Against Heresies
keyWorks.about: five books, by Eusebius's title the Refutation and Overthrow of the Knowledge Falsely So-called, against the followers of Valentinus and related teachers. By Photius's summary, the first sets out Valentinus's teaching and others' from Simon Magus to Tatian, the second refutes them, the third brings the testimony of Scripture, the fourth answers their difficulties, and the fifth draws on the Lord's parables and the apostles' letters. The third also counts the bishops of the apostles' churches and argues for four Gospels. It survives whole only in an old Latin translation; Epiphanius kept most of the first book in Greek

keyWorks.title: Letter to Florinus, On Monarchy, or That God is not the Author of Evil
keyWorks.about: to an elder at Rome whom he had seen as a boy at Polycarp's side, and who seemed to teach that God was the author of evil. It survives only in the passages Eusebius quotes, among them his memory of the place where Polycarp sat and taught

keyWorks.title: Letter to Victor of Rome on the Easter quarrel
keyWorks.about: written in the name of the Christians of Gaul over whom he presided. It held that Easter should be kept on the Lord's day, yet urged Victor not to cut off whole churches that kept an ancient custom. Eusebius quotes it

traces: About two centuries later Epiphanius of Salamis copied his opening account of the Valentinians, from the preface to the eleventh chapter of the first book, word for word into his own book against heresies. That copy is how most of the first book survives in Greek.
Eusebius quotes him often as an authority for the second century. He copies his list of Rome's bishops, his account of the four Gospels, and his letters to Florinus and to Victor.
A. Cleveland Coxe, the American editor of his English, says Tertullian takes over the first book against the Gnostics in his own Against the Valentinians.
For eighteen centuries the Valentinians were known almost only through opponents such as him, until books of their own were found in Egypt in 1945.
remembered: Hippolytus calls him "the blessed presbyter Irenæus", and Tertullian names him among those who answered the heretics as "that very exact inquirer into all doctrines".
Epiphanius calls him the elder Irenaeus, who like a noble athlete wrestled down their whole foolish system.
Eusebius says Irenaeus was well named, for he became a peacemaker in the quarrel over Easter; his name, McGiffert notes, comes from the Greek word for peace.
Theodoret of Cyrrhus lists him among his witnesses as one who enjoyed the teaching of Polycarp and became a light of the western Gauls.

uncertain: His life. Most of what is known of it comes from Eusebius, writing more than a century later, and from the few words he gives about himself. No held line says where or when he was born. Arthur McGiffert, following Lipsius, puts his birth in Asia Minor between 120 and 130; Jerome's editor Ernest Cushing Richardson gives 140 to 145; Photius's editor J. H. Freese gives about 120 to 140.

Smyrna, and the way to Gaul. He says he saw Polycarp as a boy in lower Asia; that he grew up at Smyrna is inferred from Polycarp's see. No early source says when or why he went to Gaul. Gregory of Tours, about four centuries later, says Polycarp sent him; A. Cleveland Coxe says he joined Pothinus at Lyon as his fellow pupil under Polycarp, and gives no source.

The year 177 and the martyrs' letter. The letter of the Christians of Vienne and Lyon says the imprisoned martyrs asked him to carry it to Eleutherius at Rome. It does not say he saw them die. Valesius thought he wrote it, and Coxe thinks so too; McGiffert finds that in the highest degree improbable. The letters also took a side on the new prophecy of Montanus in Phrygia, and which side is disputed: McGiffert sets out the common view that they favored it and argues, with Salmon, that they opposed it.

The account of his opponents. What the Valentinians taught is told here as he tells it, and his is an opponent's witness. He says he wrote above all against the disciples of Ptolemaeus, a bud from the school of Valentinus. The many women led astray in the district of the Rhone he lays to the followers of Marcus, one teacher among those he treats.

Rome's bishops. Whether Rome then had a single bishop at its head, historians still argue. The clause in his Rome passage that the English renders as Rome's pre-eminent authority is a famous crux: its translators say both the Latin's text and meaning are disputed and its Greek cannot be known, and Coxe adds his own polemic.
The letter to Florinus has no sure date. Lightfoot made it one of his earliest writings; Lipsius, followed by McGiffert, puts it under Victor, after Against Heresies.

His death. The early record is silent after the Easter quarrel. Jerome is the first to call him a martyr, in a later commentary on Isaiah, and Gregory of Tours gives the first full account. McGiffert holds the silence of Tertullian, Hippolytus, Eusebius and the earlier writers to be conclusive that he was not a martyr, and thinks he died, at the latest, soon after the beginning of the third century. Freese says he is said to have been martyred under Severus, but this is not regarded as certain.

Hippolytus as his pupil. Photius, in the ninth century, calls Hippolytus the pupil of Irenaeus and his book a synopsis of Irenaeus's lectures; the English translators of Against Heresies call him the author's pupil too.

The modern English. The mosaic and the one house are rendered from the Greek Epiphanius kept, not from the Latin, which is not held. The brief's small stones follow the Greek; the English made from the Latin has precious jewels. The words to Florinus are rendered from McGiffert's English, since Eusebius's Greek of that book is not held, and leave out the middle of his sentence, on Polycarp's comings and goings, his way of life, his looks and his talks to the people. Hippolytus's presbyter is rendered elder.

briefReferences: Against Heresies I.8.1, in the Greek Epiphanius copies, Panarion 31, ed. Karl Holl, with the English of Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut: the portrait of a king in small stones broken up and made into a dog or a fox, which is what the followers of Valentinus did with Scripture.
Against Heresies III.2: their claim that the truth came down by word of mouth and that they are wiser than the apostles. III.4.3: Valentinus at Rome.

Eusebius, Church History V.20, the letter to Florinus, and Against Heresies III.3.4: Polycarp heard as a boy. Church History V.5: bishop after Pothinus. V.7 and Against Heresies III.3.3, with Arthur McGiffert's note: five books, written under Eleutherius, about 180.

The letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyon, in Eusebius, Church History V.1, with McGiffert's note: the persecution of 177 on the Rhone; Pothinus, more than ninety, beaten and dead in prison; the burned bodies swept into the Rhone, so that they might have no hope of a resurrection. V.3 and V.4: the letters sent from prison to Eleutherius at Rome, carried by Irenaeus, a presbyter of the church.

World census, Irenaeus of Lyon: most of what is known of his life comes from Eusebius. Against Heresies I, preface: he read the Commentaries of the disciples of Valentinus; an abyss of madness and of blasphemy against Christ; wolves in sheep's clothing. I.1 and I.5: the perfect Aeon above and the maker of the world below.

Against Heresies I.10.1 and I.10.2, Greek and English: the faith received from the apostles; the church as if in one house, with one soul, one heart and one mouth; the churches in Germany, Spain, Egypt and Libya. I.9.4: the rule of truth received at baptism.

Against Heresies III.3.1 to III.3.3: the apostles would have given hidden mysteries to the men they left in charge of the churches; Rome's bishops down to Eleutherius, in "the twelfth place from the apostles". World census, Irenaeus of Lyon: historians still weigh his list of Rome's bishops.
Against Heresies III.1.1, III.11.8 and III.11.9: Matthew, Mark, Luke and John; four winds and four pillars; the followers of Valentinus claim more Gospels, Marcion fewer.

Eusebius, Church History V.15 and V.20: Florinus a presbyter at Rome; On Monarchy, or That God is not the Author of Evil; drawn away by the error of Valentinus; the presbyters before them, companions of the apostles, did not hand on such doctrines; the place where Polycarp sat, and his intercourse with John.

Hippolytus, Refutation of All Heresies VI.37: the blessed presbyter. Tertullian, Against the Valentinians 5: that very exact inquirer. Epiphanius, Panarion 31: his opening account copied word for word, and the Greek it keeps, with the translators' note in the English Against Heresies. World census, Valentinian and other Gnostic Christianities: known through opponents for eighteen centuries, until the finds of 1945.
Against Heresies I.9.4: who holds the rule received at baptism will know the gems but not take the fox for the king, and puts each in its place.
World census, Post-Apostolic Household-Church Christianity: his tradition.

quotationOriginals.modern: It is as if a skilled artist had carefully made a fine portrait of a king from choice small stones. Then someone broke up the man's likeness. He moved those stones, fitted them together again, and made the shape of a dog or a fox, and a poor one at that.
quotationOriginals.printed: ὅνπερ τρόπον εἴ τις βασιλέως εἰχόνος χαλῆς κατεσχευασμένης ἐπιμελῶς ἐχ Ψηφίδων ἐπισήμων ὑπὸ σοφοῦ τεχνίτου, λύσας τὴν ὑποχειμένην τοῦ ἀγϑρώπου ἰδέαν μετενέγχοι τὰς ψηφῖδας ἐχείνας χαὶ μεϑαρμόσοι χαὶ ποιήσοι μορφὴν χυνὸς ἢ ἀλῴπεχος χαὶ ταύτην φαύλως χατεσχευασμένην
quotationOriginals.work: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.8.1, Greek as Epiphanius copies it, Panarion 31, ed. Karl Holl
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: just as if one, when a beautiful image of a king has been constructed by some skilful artist out of precious jewels, should then take this likeness of the man all to pieces, should rearrange the gems, and so fit them together as to make them into the form of a dog or of a fox, and even that but poorly executed

quotationOriginals.modern: The church has received this preaching and this faith, as I said. Though it is scattered through the whole world, it guards them with care, as if it lived in one house. It believes them alike, as if it had one soul and one heart. It preaches them, teaches them and hands them on in harmony, as if it had one mouth.
quotationOriginals.printed: τοῦτο τὸ χήρυγμα παρειληφυῖα χαὶ ταύτην τὴν πίστιν ὡς προἔφαμεν ἡ ἐχχλησία, χαίπερ ἐν ὅλῳ τῷ χόσμῳ διεσπαρμένη, ἐπιμελῶς φυλάσσει: ὡς ἕνα οἶχον οἰχοῦσα χαὶ ὁμοίως πιστεύει τούτοις ὡς μίαν ψυχὴν χαὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἔχουσα χαρδίαν χαὶ συμφώνως ταῦτα χηρύσσει χαὶ διδάσχει χαὶ παραδίδωσιν ὡς ἕν στόμα χεχτημένη
quotationOriginals.work: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.10.2, Greek as Epiphanius copies it, Panarion 31, ed. Karl Holl
quotationOriginals.englishPrinted: As I have already observed, the Church, having received this preaching and this faith, although scattered throughout the whole world, yet, as if occupying but one house, carefully preserves it. She also believes these points [of doctrine] just as if she had but one soul, and one and the same heart, and she proclaims them, and teaches them, and hands them down, with perfect harmony, as if she possessed only one mouth.

quotationOriginals.modern: the twelfth place from the apostles
quotationOriginals.printed: Eleutherius does now, in the twelfth place from the apostles, hold the inheritance of the episcopate.
quotationOriginals.work: Irenaeus, Against Heresies III.3.3, tr. Alexander Roberts and W. H. Rambaut

quotationOriginals.modern: I remember that time more clearly than recent years. For what boys learn grows with the mind and becomes one with it. So I can describe the very place where the blessed Polycarp sat as he taught. And I can tell how he spoke of his time with John and the others who had seen the Lord.
quotationOriginals.printed: I remember the events of that time more clearly than those of recent years. For what boys learn, growing with their mind, becomes joined with it; so that I am able to describe the very place in which the blessed Polycarp sat as he discoursed, and his goings out and his comings in, and the manner of his life, and his physical appearance, and his discourses to the people, and the accounts which he gave of his intercourse with John and with the others who had seen the Lord.
